claim: Published papers receive more citations if they first appeared as preprints.
source: In addition to allowing researchers to share their work independently of publication at a traditional journal, there is evidence that published papers receive more citations if they first appeared as preprints (Fu and Hughey, 2019; Fraser et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies that examined citation patterns.

claim: Some journals search preprint servers to solicit submissions.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to sources documenting this practice.

claim: Relatively little is known about who is benefiting from the growth of preprints or how this new approach to publishing is affecting different populations of researchers.
source: However, relatively little is known about who is benefiting from the growth of preprints or how this new approach to publishing is affecting different populations of researchers (Penfold and Polka, 2020).

claim: Studies have found bias in favor of wealthy, English-speaking countries in citation count.

claim: 17 countries met the criteria for 'contributor countries' (appearing on at least 50 international preprints but as senior author on less than 20% of them).
source: For this analysis, we defined a contributor country as one that has contributed to at least 50 international preprints but appears in the senior author position of less than 20% of them. (We excluded countries with less than 50 preprints to minimize the effect of dynamics that could be explained by countries with just one or two labs that frequently worked with international collaborators.) 17 countries met these criteria (Figure 3—figure supplement 1): for example, of the 84 international preprints that had an author with an affiliation in Uganda, only 5 (6%) had an author from Uganda in the senior author position.

claim: Four links between contributor countries and senior-author countries were statistically significant: Australia and Bangladesh, the UK and Thailand, the UK and Greece, and Australia and Vietnam.
source: Using Fisher's exact test (see Methods), we found four links between contributor countries and senior-author countries that were significant (Figure 3—source data 2). The strongest link is between Bangladesh and Australia: of the 82 international preprints with an author from Bangladesh, 22 list a senior author with an affiliation in Australia. Authors in Vietnam appear with disproportionate frequency on preprints with a senior author in Australia as well (9 of 67 preprints). The other two links are to senior authors in the UK, with contributing authors from Thailand (50 of 187 preprints) and Greece (41 of 155 preprints).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The US accounts for 61.0% of preprints published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS).
source: 33 of the 63 significant links were between a journal and the US: the US is listed as the senior author on 41.7% of published preprints, but accounts for 74.5% of all bioRxiv preprints published in Cell, 72.7% of preprints published in Science, and 61.0% of those published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) (Figure 5b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and referenced figure.

claim: The US is by far the most highly represented country by number of preprints, followed distantly by the UK and Germany.
source: We show that the US is by far the most highly represented country by number of preprints, followed distantly by the UK and Germany.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The US and the UK are overrepresented on bioRxiv even after accounting for their overall scientific output.
source: By adjusting preprint counts by each country's overall scientific output, we were able to develop a 'bioRxiv adoption' score (Figure 2), which showed the US and the UK are overrepresented while countries such as Turkey, Iran and Malaysia are underrepresented even after accounting for their comparatively low scientific output.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and referenced figure.

claim: Turkey, Iran, and Malaysia are underrepresented on bioRxiv even after accounting for their comparatively low scientific output.
source: By adjusting preprint counts by each country's overall scientific output, we were able to develop a 'bioRxiv adoption' score (Figure 2), which showed the US and the UK are overrepresented while countries such as Turkey, Iran and Malaysia are underrepresented even after accounting for their comparatively low scientific output.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and referenced figure.

claim: Those reading bioRxiv are reviewing a biased sample of worldwide scholarship.
source: Our results make it clear that those reading bioRxiv (or soliciting submissions from the platform) are reviewing a biased sample of worldwide scholarship.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing unequal representation of countries on bioRxiv.

claim: The current corpus of bioRxiv preprints contains the same familiar disparities observed in published literature.
source: While there are many reasons these dynamics could arise, it is worth noting that the current corpus of bioRxiv preprints contains the same familiar disparities observed in published literature (Mammides et al., 2016; Burgman et al., 2015; Wong et al., 2014; González-Alcaide et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and citations to studies documenting similar disparities in published literature.

claim: The three characteristics of contributor countries (low international collaboration count, high international collaboration rate, low international senior author rate) are strongly correlated with each other.
source: Critically, we found the three characteristics of contributor countries (low international collaboration count, high international collaboration rate, low international senior author rate) are strongly correlated with each other (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and referenced figure.

claim: If a country fits even one of the contributor country criteria, they are more likely to fit the other two as well.
source: When looking at international collaboration using pairwise combinations of these three measurements, countries fall along tidy gradients (Figure 3—figure supplement 3)—which means not only that they can be used to delineate properties of contributor countries, but that if a country fits even one of these criteria, they are more likely to fit the other two as well.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the strong correlations observed between the three characteristics.

claim: There is a positive correlation at the country level between downloads per preprint and publication rate.
source: Second, we found numerous country-level differences in preprint outcomes, including a positive correlation at the country level between downloads per preprint and publication rate (Figure 4c).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and referenced figure.

claim: The average Brazilian preprint receives 37% fewer downloads than the average Dutch preprint.
source: If one of the goals of preprinting one's work is to solicit feedback from the community (Sarabipour et al., 2019; Sever et al., 2019), what are the implications of the average Brazilian preprint receiving 37% fewer downloads than the average Dutch preprint?
evidence: The claim is inferred from data on downloads per preprint by country.

claim: Countries that get more downloads also tend to have higher publication rates.
source: What role does language play in outcomes, and why do countries that get more downloads also tend to have higher publication rates?
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing a correlation between downloads and publication rates.

claim: Dozens of journal–country links disproportionately favored the US and UK.
source: We also found some journals had particularly strong affinities for preprints from some countries over others: even when accounting for differing publication rates across countries, we found dozens of journal–country links that disproportionately favored the US and UK.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Journals can embrace preprints while still perpetuating some of the imbalances that preprints could be theoretically alleviating.
source: While it's possible this finding is coincidental, it demonstrates that journals can embrace preprints while still perpetuating some of the imbalances that preprints could be theoretically alleviating.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing disproportionate publication of preprints from certain countries.

claim: bioRxiv is the preprint server most broadly integrated into the traditional publishing system.
source: We chose to focus on bioRxiv for several reasons: primarily, bioRxiv is the preprint server most broadly integrated into the traditional publishing system (Barsh et al., 2016; Vence, 2017; eLife, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to sources documenting bioRxiv's integration.

claim: bioRxiv currently holds the largest collection of biology preprints.
source: In addition, bioRxiv currently holds the largest collection of biology preprints, with metadata available in a format we were already equipped to ingest (Abdill and Blekhman, 2019c).
evidence: The claim is supported by data on the number of preprints hosted by bioRxiv.

claim: bioRxiv is one of the few preprint servers with an automated method for detecting when a preprint has been published.
source: Comparing publication rates between repositories would also be difficult, particularly because bioRxiv is one of the few with an automated method for detecting when a preprint has been published.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of bioRxiv's features.

claim: BioRxiv accepts submissions only in English.
source: Second, this 'worldwide' analysis of preprints is explicitly biased toward English-language publishing. BioRxiv accepts submissions only in English, and the primary motivation for this work was the attention being paid to bioRxiv by organizations based mostly in the US and western Europe.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of bioRxiv's submission policies.

claim: Bibliometrics databases such as Scopus and Web of Science have well-documented biases in favor of English-language publications.
source: In addition, bibliometrics databases such as Scopus and Web of Science have well-documented biases in favor of English-language publications (Mongeon and Paul-Hus, 2016; Archambault et al., 2006; de Moya-Anegón et al., 2007), which could have an effect on observed publication rates and the bioRxiv adoption scores that depend on scientific output derived from Scopus.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies documenting these biases.

claim: 4,985 preprints (7.3%) could not be confidently assigned a country of origin.
source: There were also 4985 preprints (7.3%) for which we were not able to confidently assign a country of origin.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The most prolific countries were underrepresented in the 'unknown' category, compared to the 148 other countries with at least one author.
source: An evaluation of these (see Methods) showed that the most prolific countries were also underrepresented in the 'unknown' category, compared to the 148 other countries with at least one author.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The preprint counts for countries with comparatively low participation may be slightly higher than reported.
source: While it is impractical to draw country-specific conclusions from this, it suggests that the preprint counts for countries with comparatively low participation may be slightly higher than reported, an issue that may be exacerbated in more granular analyses, such as at the institutional level.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the underrepresentation of less prolific countries in the 'unknown' category.

claim: On average, genomics preprints are downloaded twice as many times as microbiology preprints.
source: Country-level differences in metrics such as downloads and publication rate may also be confounded with field-level differences: on average, genomics preprints are downloaded twice as many times as microbiology preprints (Abdill and Blekhman, 2019b), for example, so countries with a disproportionate number of preprints in a particular field could receive more downloads due to choice of topic, rather than country of origin.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study documenting this difference.

claim: Countries with a disproportionate number of preprints in a particular field could receive more downloads due to choice of topic, rather than country of origin.
source: Country-level differences in metrics such as downloads and publication rate may also be confounded with field-level differences: on average, genomics preprints are downloaded twice as many times as microbiology preprints (Abdill and Blekhman, 2019b), for example, so countries with a disproportionate number of preprints in a particular field could receive more downloads due to choice of topic, rather than country of origin.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that different fields have different download rates.

claim: Preprint outcomes reflect particularly large differences between countries: comparatively wealthy countries in Europe and North America post more preprints, which are downloaded more frequently, published more consistently, and favored by the largest and most well-known journals in biology.
source: In summary, we find country-level participation on bioRxiv differs significantly from existing patterns in scientific publishing. Preprint outcomes reflect particularly large differences between countries: comparatively wealthy countries in Europe and North America post more preprints, which are downloaded more frequently, published more consistently, and favored by the largest and most well-known journals in biology.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The last individual in the author list is considered by convention in the life sciences to be the 'senior author' who supervised the work.
source: First, we attributed each preprint to a single country, using the affiliation of the last individual in the author list, considered by convention in the life sciences to be the 'senior author' who supervised the work (see Methods).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and convention.

claim: Among the 59,562 preprints for which the country was known for the first and last author, 7,965 (13.4%) preprints included a first author associated with a different country than the senior author.
source: Among the 59,562 preprints for which the country was known for the first and last author, 7965 (13.4%) preprints included a first author associated with a different country than the senior author.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 91% of publications indicated a corresponding author that was in the first- or last-author position.
source: Throughout the analysis, we define the 'senior author' for each preprint as the author appearing last in the author list, a longstanding practice in biomedical literature (Riesenberg, 1990; Buehring et al., 2007) corroborated by a 2003 study, which found that 91% of publications indicated a corresponding author that was in the first- or last-author position (Mattsson et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study documenting this finding.

claim: The complete-normalized preprint counts are almost identical to the counts distributed based on straight counting (Pearson's r = 0.9971, p=4.48 × 10−197).
source: We found the complete-normalized preprint counts to be almost identical to the counts distributed based on straight counting (Pearson's r = 0.9971, p=4.48 × 10−197).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Senior authors are at least an accurate proxy for the overall number of individual authors, at the country level.
source: While there are numerous proposals for proportioning differing levels of recognition to authors at different positions in the author list (e.g. Hagen, 2013; Kim and Diesner, 2015), the close link between the complete-normalized count and the count based on senior authorship indicates that senior authors are at least an accurate proxy for the overall number of individual authors, at the country level.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the high correlation between complete-normalized and senior author counts.

claim: Authors were responsible for about one-third of a preprint in 2014, but less than one-fourth of a preprint as of 2019.
source: When computing the average authors per paper, the harmonic mean is used to capture the average 'contribution' of an author, as in Glänzel and Schubert, 2005—in short, this shows that authors were responsible for about one-third of a preprint in 2014, but less than one-fourth of a preprint as of 2019.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and a citation to a methodological reference.

claim: Countries with fewer international collaborations also tend to appear as senior author on a smaller proportion of those preprints.
source: First, countries with fewer international collaborations also tend to appear as senior author on a smaller proportion of those preprints (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and referenced figure.

claim: There is a negative correlation between total international collaborations and international collaboration rate.
source: Second, we also observed a negative correlation between total international collaborations and international collaboration rate – that is, the proportion of preprints a country contributes to that include at least one contributor from another country (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and referenced figure.

claim: Countries with mostly international preprints also tended to have fewer international collaborations than other countries.
source: This indicates that countries with mostly international preprints (Figure 3b) also tended to have fewer international collaborations (Figure 3c) than other countries.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the negative correlation between international collaboration rate and total international collaborations.

claim: There is a negative correlation between international collaboration rate and the proportion of international preprints for which a country appears as senior author.
source: Third, we found a negative correlation between international collaboration rate and the proportion of international preprints for which a country appears as senior author (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c), demonstrating that countries that appear mostly on international preprints (Figure 3b) are less likely to appear as senior author of those preprints (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and referenced figure.

claim: Countries that appear mostly on international preprints are less likely to appear as senior author of those preprints.
source: Third, we found a negative correlation between international collaboration rate and the proportion of international preprints for which a country appears as senior author (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c), demonstrating that countries that appear mostly on international preprints (Figure 3b) are less likely to appear as senior author of those preprints (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the negative correlation between international collaboration rate and senior authorship rate.

claim: González-Alcaide et al., 2017 found countries ranked lower on the Human Development Index participated more frequently in international collaborations.
source: Similar patterns have been observed in previous studies: González-Alcaide et al., 2017 found countries ranked lower on the Human Development Index participated more frequently in international collaborations, and a review of oncology papers found that researchers from low- and middle-income countries collaborated on randomized control trials, but rarely as senior author (Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study documenting this finding.

claim: A review of oncology papers found that researchers from low- and middle-income countries collaborated on randomized control trials, but rarely as senior author.
source: Similar patterns have been observed in previous studies: González-Alcaide et al., 2017 found countries ranked lower on the Human Development Index participated more frequently in international collaborations, and a review of oncology papers found that researchers from low- and middle-income countries collaborated on randomized control trials, but rarely as senior author (Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study documenting this finding.

claim: There is a modest correlation (Spearman's rho = 0.295, p=0.0489) between a country's preprint publication rate and the rate at which publishers in that country assigned DOIs.
source: There are 45 countries that overlap between our analysis and that of Boudry and Chartron, 2017. Of these, we found a modest correlation (Spearman's rho = 0.295, p=0.0489) between a country's preprint publication rate and the rate at which publishers in that country assigned DOIs (Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Countries with higher rates of DOI issuance also tend to have higher observed rates of preprint publication.
source: This indicates that countries with higher rates of DOI issuance (for publications dating back to 1955) also tend to have higher observed rates of preprint publication.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between DOI issuance rates and preprint publication rates.

claim: The study was submitted to the University of Minnesota Institutional Review Board (study #00008793), which determined the work did not qualify as human subjects research and did not require IRB oversight.
source: This study was submitted to the University of Minnesota Institutional Review Board (study #00008793), which determined the work did not qualify as human subjects research and did not require IRB oversight.
evidence: The claim is a statement of fact about the ethical review process.

claim: 95 preprints were excluded because the bioRxiv website repeatedly returned errors when trying to collect the metadata.
source: In addition, 95 preprints were excluded because the bioRxiv website repeatedly returned errors when we tried to collect the metadata, leaving a total of 67,885 preprints in the analysis.
evidence: The claim describes a data collection issue.

claim: There were 2,409 manuscripts (3.6%) for which affiliation data could not be scraped for at least one author.
source: Of these, there were 2409 manuscripts (3.6%) for which we were unable to scrape affiliation data for at least one author, including 137 preprints with no affiliation information for any author.
evidence: The claim describes a data collection issue.

claim: 137 preprints had no affiliation information for any author.
source: Of these, there were 2409 manuscripts (3.6%) for which we were unable to scrape affiliation data for at least one author, including 137 preprints with no affiliation information for any author.
evidence: The claim describes a data collection issue.

claim: The bioRxiv API only includes the corresponding author's institutional affiliation.
source: bioRxiv maintains an application programmatic interface (API) that provides machine-readable data about their holdings. However, the information it exposes about authors and their affiliations is not as complete as the information available from the website itself, and only the corresponding author's institutional affiliation is included (https://api.biorxiv.org/).
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of the bioRxiv API's features.

claim: It is possible, if not likely, that the publication of many preprints goes undetected by bioRxiv's system.
source: All data on published preprints was pulled directly from bioRxiv. However, it is also possible, if not likely, that the publication of many preprints goes undetected by its system.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the limitations of bioRxiv's detection system.

claim: Fraser et al., 2020 found most published preprints had already been picked up by bioRxiv's detection process.
source: Fraser et al., 2020 developed a method of searching for published preprints in Scopus and Crossref databases and found most had already been picked up by bioRxiv's detection process, though bioRxiv states that preprints published with new titles or authors can go undetected (https://www.biorxiv.org/about-biorxiv), and preliminary data suggests this may affect thousands of preprints (Abdill and Blekhman, 2019b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study documenting this finding.

claim: bioRxiv states that preprints published with new titles or authors can go undetected.
source: Fraser et al., 2020 developed a method of searching for published preprints in Scopus and Crossref databases and found most had already been picked up by bioRxiv's detection process, though bioRxiv states that preprints published with new titles or authors can go undetected (https://www.biorxiv.org/about-biorxiv), and preliminary data suggests this may affect thousands of preprints (Abdill and Blekhman, 2019b).
evidence: The claim is based on information from bioRxiv's website.

claim: Preliminary data suggests undetected publications may affect thousands of preprints.
source: Fraser et al., 2020 developed a method of searching for published preprints in Scopus and Crossref databases and found most had already been picked up by bioRxiv's detection process, though bioRxiv states that preprints published with new titles or authors can go undetected (https://www.biorxiv.org/about-biorxiv), and preliminary data suggests this may affect thousands of preprints (Abdill and Blekhman, 2019b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to preliminary data.

claim: Boudry and Chartron, 2017 found DOI assignment varied widely based on the country of the publisher.
source: Boudry and Chartron, 2017 examined papers from 2015 indexed by PubMed and found DOI assignment varied widely based on the country of the publisher.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study documenting this finding.

claim: 96% of publications in Germany had a DOI.
source: 96% of publications in Germany had a DOI, for example, plus 98% of UK publications and more than 99% of Brazilian publications.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study documenting this finding.

claim: 98% of UK publications had a DOI.
source: 96% of publications in Germany had a DOI, for example, plus 98% of UK publications and more than 99% of Brazilian publications.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study documenting this finding.

claim: More than 99% of Brazilian publications had a DOI.
source: 96% of publications in Germany had a DOI, for example, plus 98% of UK publications and more than 99% of Brazilian publications.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study documenting this finding.

claim: Only 31% of papers published in China had DOIs.
source: However, only 31% of papers published in China had DOIs, and just 2% (33 out of 1582) of papers published in Russia.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study documenting this finding.

claim: Just 2% (33 out of 1582) of papers published in Russia had DOIs.
source: However, only 31% of papers published in China had DOIs, and just 2% (33 out of 1582) of papers published in Russia.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study documenting this finding.

claim: The last author is considered by convention in the life sciences to be the 'senior author' who supervised the work, a practice corroborated by a 2003 study.
source: Throughout the analysis, we define the 'senior author' for each preprint as the author appearing last in the author list, a longstanding practice in biomedical literature (Riesenberg, 1990; Buehring et al., 2007) corroborated by a 2003 study, which found that 91% of publications indicated a corresponding author that was in the first- or last-author position (Mattsson et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies documenting this practice.

claim: Prior to correction, 23,158 (17%) distinct affiliation strings were categorized as 'unknown', associated with 71,947 authors.
source: Prior to correction, 23,158 (17%) distinct affiliation strings were categorized as 'unknown,' associated with 71,947 authors.
evidence: The claim describes the data before manual corrections.

claim: After manual corrections, there were 20,099 unknown affiliation strings associated with 51,855 authors.
source: After manual corrections, there were 20,099 unknown affiliation strings associated with 51,855 authors.
evidence: The claim describes the data after manual corrections.

claim: 12,487 institutional assignments were corrected, affecting 52,037 author entries (10.6%).
source: In total, 12,487 institutional assignments were corrected, affecting 52,037 author entries (10.6%).
evidence: The claim describes the extent of manual corrections.

claim: Prior to the corrections, the country-level accuracy of ROR assignments in a random sample (n = 488) was 92.2 ± 2.4%, at a 95% confidence interval.
source: Prior to the corrections, an evaluation of the ROR assignments in a random sample (n = 488) found the country-level accuracy was 92.2 ± 2.4%, at a 95% confidence interval.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a random sample evaluation.

claim: After an initial round of corrections, the country-level accuracy improved to 96.5 ± 1.6%.
source: After an initial round of corrections, the country-level accuracy improved to 96.5 ± 1.6%.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a random sample evaluation.

claim: After another round of corrections, the country-level accuracy of the corrected affiliations was 95.7 ± 2.2%.
source: After another round of corrections that assigned countries to 14,690 authors in the 'unknown' category, we pulled another random sample of corrected affiliations—using a 95% confidence interval, the sample size required to detect 96.5% assignment accuracy with a 2% margin of error was calculated to be 325 (Naing et al., 2006). Manually evaluating the country assignments of this sample showed the country-level accuracy of the corrected affiliations was 95.7 ± 2.2%.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a random sample evaluation.

claim: The 27 most prolific countries account for 95.3% of categorized preprints.
source: Among the successfully classified preprints, the distribution across countries is heavily skewed—the 27 most prolific countries (15%) account for 95.3% of categorized preprints.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Within a sample of 307 uncategorized preprints, preprints with a senior author in the bottom 148 countries were present at a prevalence of 12.6 ± 3.9%.
source: Using a 95% confidence interval and a precision of 0.00235 (half the prevalence), the sample size (with correction for a finite population of 4,985) was calculated to be 307 (Naing et al., 2006). Within this sample, we found that preprints with a senior author in the bottom 148 countries were present at a prevalence of 12.6 ± 3.9%.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a random sample evaluation.
